newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Record Australian sugar sales seen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Record Australian sugar sales seen.

text.p: Australia was headed for record raw sugar sales from its big 1996 crop as new season sugar got off to a good start, David Rutledge, chief executive of Queensland Sugar Corp (QSC), told Reuters on Wednesday.
Rutledge also said that low world prices, which cast a pall over Australia's record production in 1996, could begin to pick up possibly before the end of the 1997 season.
This could occur as supply began to contract, he said in an interview at the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) Outlook conference.
With QSC's international marketing programme for the 1996 raw sugar crop now almost over, attention was turning to the new crop, Rutledge told Reuters.
The ABARE forecast of 5.5 million tonnes of raw sugar for 1997/98 ending June 30, up from 5.3 million tonnes in 1996/97, looked "plausible", he said.
The crop was in the ground and growing well with good seasonal conditions, he said.
"But current prices would not encourage significant expansion," he said.
Present expansion momentum would not be turned off overnight, but at current prices could begin to to slacken as cane growers re-thought expansion plans, he said.
The 1996 crop was now very substantially committed for both tonnages and price, with shipments running high, he said.
Sales to new markets continued, with recent cargoes shipped to Morocco and Iran.
However, sales to the established market in China were down.
China continued to be a difficult market as the Chinese authorities very substantially blocked imports to support domestic price and industry, he said.
Sales to China from other sugar producers would also be down, he said.
About 40,000 tonnes were sold to each of the new refineries in Saudi Arabia and Indonesia from the 1996 crop.
But 1996 crop sales were not made to the refinery in Dubai, despite substantial sales the year before, he said.
"We've chosen not to meet the competition from other origins including Brazil. It's almost always a price matter," he said.
QSC could have chosen to meet the competition but believed it could do better elsewhere, he said.
A continuation of prices at current low levels would not encourage significant expansion of production, he said.

Prices in 1996/97 fell to an average of 10.8 US cents a pound from 12.5 cents in 1995/96 and from 13.9 cents a lb the year before. ABARE has forecast that prices will fall further to 10.3 cents a pound in 1997/98.
Rutledge said the possibility of prices continuing to fall could not be ruled out in the short-term.

"But if Australian producers are beginning to feel the pain at these price levels ... that would suggest that prices ought not go substantially lower ... at these levels others would be feeling it to an even greater extent," he said.
Prices were unlikely to go substantially lower in the medium term and could start to pick up earlier than the end of the 1997 season, he said.
While ABARE's forecast 5.5 million tonne crop for 1997/98 was plausible, the agency's further projections, to 6.4 million tonnes in year 2001/02, should not be seen in isolation from price, he said.
"It depends very much on what happens in China, on whether the Russians are able to absorb significant purchases, on what happens to crops around the world," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
